na_count[na_count > 0]

## Data Processing

```{r}
# Verify loan_is_bad coding
table(data$loan_is_bad, useNA = "ifany")

# Baseline bad rate
overall_bad_rate <- mean(data$loan_is_bad, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Overall Bad Rate (Baseline):", round(overall_bad_rate * 100, 2), "%\n")

# Pre-compute net_profit and credit loss at loan level
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    net_profit          = total_pymnt - funded_amnt,
    individual_credit_loss = ifelse(net_profit < 0, -net_profit, 0)
  )
```

---

## Q1a. Policy Definition

To address the business objective of minimising losses while maintaining profitability, we define two
rule-based policies grounded in standard credit-risk practice:

**Policy A (Conservative)**  
Criteria: Grade A–C, DTI < 35, Delinquencies (2 yrs) = 0.  
Targets "prime" borrowers only. A 35 % DTI threshold is a standard industry marker of financial
headroom; zero recent delinquencies enforces strict credit-quality control.

**Policy B (Aggressive)**  
Criteria: Grade A–E, DTI < 50, Delinquencies (2 yrs) ≤ 2.  
Extends credit to sub-prime borrowers (Grades D–E). A 50 % DTI is the regulatory ceiling for
acceptable debt burden; allowing up to two recent delinquencies admits borrowers with minor credit
blemishes. Policy B aims to maximise portfolio size and total interest income, relying on higher
margins from Grades D–E to absorb elevated default losses.

```{r}
df <- data %>%
  mutate(
    approve_A = ifelse(grade %in% c("A","B","C") & dti < 35 & delinq_2yrs == 0,  1, 0),
    approve_B = ifelse(grade %in% c("A","B","C","D","E") & dti < 50 & delinq_2yrs <= 2, 1, 0)
  )

cat("Policy A – approved loans:", sum(df$approve_A), "\n")
cat("Policy B – approved loans:", sum(df$approve_B), "\n")
cat("Total loans in dataset:   ", nrow(df), "\n")
```

---

## Q1b. Evaluation Metric and Hypotheses

### Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC): Total Net Profit

The primary evaluation criterion is **Total Net Profit**, defined as the sum of (amount received –
amount funded) across all approved loans:

$$\text{Total Net Profit} = \sum_{i \in \text{Approved}} (\text{total_pymnt}_i - \text{funded_amnt}_i)$$

This metric directly captures the business objective: it rewards policies that generate high interest
income and penalises policies that incur credit losses, all on a single monetary scale. A policy that
approves many loans but suffers heavy defaults will show a lower (or negative) Net Profit, while one
that is too conservative will also score poorly by forfeiting profitable loans.



### Hypotheses

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{Profit},A} = \mu_{\text{Profit},B}$$
$$H_1: \mu_{\text{Profit},B} > \mu_{\text{Profit},A}$$

where $\mu_{\text{Profit}}$ is the mean net profit per approved loan under each policy.  
A one-sided Welch *t*-test is used because net profit is a continuous variable and population
variances cannot be assumed equal.

---

## Q1c. Policy Comparison

```{r}
# ── Helper: business value summary ──────────────────────────────────────────
calc_business_value <- function(df, approve_col, label) {
  approved <- df %>% filter(.data[[approve_col]] == 1)
  rejected <- df %>% filter(.data[[approve_col]] == 0)
  rejected_good <- rejected %>% filter(loan_is_bad == 0)

  tibble(
    Policy           = label,
    Total_Approved   = nrow(approved),
    Approval_Rate    = nrow(approved) / nrow(df),
    Bad_Rate         = mean(approved$loan_is_bad),
    Total_Net_Profit = sum(approved$net_profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean_Net_Profit  = mean(approved$net_profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    Credit_Loss_FN   = sum(approved$individual_credit_loss, na.rm = TRUE),
    Opp_Cost_FP      = sum(rejected_good$net_profit, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

perf_A    <- calc_business_value(df, "approve_A", "Policy A")
perf_B    <- calc_business_value(df, "approve_B", "Policy B")
perf_Base <- tibble(
  Policy           = "Baseline (All Approved)",
  Total_Approved   = nrow(df),
  Approval_Rate    = 1,
  Bad_Rate         = mean(df$loan_is_bad, na.rm = TRUE),
  Total_Net_Profit = sum(df$net_profit, na.rm = TRUE),
  Mean_Net_Profit  = mean(df$net_profit, na.rm = TRUE),
  Credit_Loss_FN   = sum(df$individual_credit_loss, na.rm = TRUE),
  Opp_Cost_FP      = 0
)

business_comparison <- bind_rows(perf_A, perf_B, perf_Base)
print(business_comparison)
```

```{r}
# ── Summary statistics ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cat("=== Summary Statistics ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Policy A – Approved: %d (%.1f%%), Bad Rate: %.2f%%, Total Net Profit: $%.2fM, Mean Net Profit: $%.0f\n",
    perf_A$Total_Approved, perf_A$Approval_Rate*100,
    perf_A$Bad_Rate*100,
    perf_A$Total_Net_Profit/1e6,
    perf_A$Mean_Net_Profit))

cat(sprintf("Policy B – Approved: %d (%.1f%%), Bad Rate: %.2f%%, Total Net Profit: $%.2fM, Mean Net Profit: $%.0f\n",
    perf_B$Total_Approved, perf_B$Approval_Rate*100,
    perf_B$Bad_Rate*100,
    perf_B$Total_Net_Profit/1e6,
    perf_B$Mean_Net_Profit))

cat(sprintf("\nProfit difference (B – A): $%.2fM\n",
    (perf_B$Total_Net_Profit - perf_A$Total_Net_Profit)/1e6))
cat(sprintf("Additional credit loss under B vs A: $%.2fM\n",
    (perf_B$Credit_Loss_FN - perf_A$Credit_Loss_FN)/1e6))
cat(sprintf("Opportunity cost avoided by B vs A:  $%.2fM\n",
    (perf_A$Opp_Cost_FP - perf_B$Opp_Cost_FP)/1e6))
```

```{r}
# ── One-sided Welch t-test on per-loan net profit (OEC) ─────────────────────
profit_A <- df %>% filter(approve_A == 1) %>% pull(net_profit)
profit_B <- df %>% filter(approve_B == 1) %>% pull(net_profit)

t_result <- t.test(profit_B, profit_A,
                   alternative = "greater",   # H1: mean profit B > mean profit A
                   var.equal   = FALSE)
print(t_result)

cat(sprintf("\np-value: %.4f  |  Decision: %s\n",
    t_result$p.value,
    ifelse(t_result$p.value < 0.05,
           "Reject H0 – Policy B generates significantly higher mean net profit",
           "Fail to reject H0")))
```

```{r}
# ── Confusion matrix (for reference; Positive = Default) ────────────────────
# Convention used here: rejecting a loan = "predicting bad"
# TP = Rejected & Bad  |  FP = Rejected & Good (opportunity cost)
# TN = Approved & Good |  FN = Approved & Bad  (credit loss)

calc_cm <- function(policy_decision, actual_bad) {
  table(Decision = ifelse(policy_decision == 1, "Approved", "Rejected"),
        Actual   = ifelse(actual_bad == 1, "Bad", "Good"))
}

cat("\nConfusion Matrix – Policy A\n")
print(calc_cm(df$approve_A, df$loan_is_bad))

cat("\nConfusion Matrix – Policy B\n")
print(calc_cm(df$approve_B, df$loan_is_bad))
```

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
# ── Visualisation 1a: Total Net Profit (OEC) ────────────────────────────────
p_profit <- ggplot(business_comparison, aes(x = Policy, y = Total_Net_Profit / 1e6)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("$%.1fM", Total_Net_Profit / 1e6)),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title    = "Figure 1a: Total Net Profit by Policy (OEC)",
       subtitle = "Policy B generates the highest total net profit",
       y = "Total Net Profit (USD Millions)", x = "Policy") +
  theme_minimal()

# ── Visualisation 1b: Bad Rate  ──────────────────────────────────
p_badrate <- ggplot(business_comparison, aes(x = Policy, y = Bad_Rate)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.7, width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", Bad_Rate * 100)),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title    = "Figure 1b: Bad Rate Comparison",
       subtitle = "Policy B has a higher default rate risk monitoring required",
       y = "Bad Rate", x = "Policy") +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p_profit, p_badrate, ncol = 2)
```

```{r}
# ── Visualisation 2: Cost structure ─────────────────────────────────────────
cost_data <- business_comparison %>%
  filter(Policy %in% c("Policy A", "Policy B")) %>%
  select(Policy, Opp_Cost_FP, Credit_Loss_FN) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Policy, names_to = "Cost_Type", values_to = "Amount")

p_costs <- ggplot(cost_data, aes(x = Policy, y = Amount / 1e6, fill = Cost_Type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Opp_Cost_FP" = "darkorange", "Credit_Loss_FN" = "darkred"),
    labels = c("Opportunity Cost (rejected good loans)", "Credit Loss (approved defaults)")
  ) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("$%.1fM", Amount / 1e6)),
          position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
          vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title    = "Figure 1c: Cost Structure: Opportunity Cost vs. Credit Loss",
       subtitle = "Policy A sacrifices large opportunity cost to achieve lower credit loss",
       y = "USD Millions", x = "Policy", fill = "Cost Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

print(p_costs)
```

### Interpretation

**Statistical significance:** The one-sided Welch *t*-test shows that the mean net profit per approved
loan under Policy B is significantly higher than under Policy A (*p* < 0.05), leading us to **reject
H₀**.

**Business interpretation:**

- Policy B approves a substantially larger share of applicants, capturing profitable Grade D–E loans
  that Policy A foregoes. The higher interest margins on these loans more than offset the additional
  credit losses incurred.
- Policy A's excessive conservatism incurs a large **opportunity cost** (profitable good loans
  wrongly rejected), which more than negates its credit-loss savings.

**Conclusion:** Policy B is preferred on the  OEC (Total Net Profit). Any deployment should
be accompanied by portfolio-level Bad Rate ceilings as a risk guardrail.

---

## Q1d. Limitations

1. **Survivorship bias:** The dataset includes only loans previously approved by LendingClub. We
   cannot observe outcomes for applicants who were rejected historically but might qualify under
   Policy B, so the true Bad Rate under Policy B may be underestimated.

2. **No true randomisation:** This is a retrospective back-test, not a prospective RCT. Selection
   effects mean that causal claims about policy outcomes are not warranted.

3. **Static behaviour assumption:** The analysis assumes borrower behaviour is fixed. In practice,
   a more permissive policy may attract riskier applicants through adverse selection, inflating the
   real-world Bad Rate beyond what historical data suggests.

4. **Temporal confounding:** Macroeconomic conditions (interest rates, unemployment) prevalent
   during 2012–2013 may not persist, making extrapolation of profit estimates uncertain.

5. **Single-period view:** Net profit as computed does not discount for the time value of money or
   for the cost of capital, which may favour shorter-tenor loans unfairly.
```
